LAST UPDATED: 22 July 2026 Detox Your Home is a free Victorian Government service for disposing of hazardous household chemicals safely. Events are staffed by trained chemists. Any Victorian can attend any event, but you must register online first. Detox Your Home accepts acids and alkalis, aerosols, spray paint, automotive paint, bleach, brake

online first. insect sprays, pesticides, rat poison and other poisons, machine oil, nail polish remover, oven cleaner, photographic chemicals, pool chemicals, rust remover, transmission fluid, turpentine, paint thinners and strippers, wood preservatives and finishes, and non-halon fire extinguishers. Detox Your Home does not accept motor oil, gas bottles or

preservatives and finishes, and non-halon fire extinguishers. Detox Your Home does not accept motor oil, gas bottles or cylinders (other than small camping canisters), household paint, or yellow halon fire extinguishers. Heating oil, mercury thermometers and thermostats, helium canisters and propane cylinders need approval before you bring them.

oil, mercury thermometers and thermostats, helium canisters and propane cylinders need approval before you bring them. To transport chemicals to an event, put them in an empty car boot or tray, keep them in their original packaging where possible, and label repackaged or unknown substances. FOGO bin is intended for accepted food scraps and garden clippings. TITLE: Recycling glass in Victoria SOURCE ORGANISATION: Department of Energy, Environment and Climate Action (DEECA), Victorian Government SOURCE PAGE: Recycling glass in Victoria SOURCE URL: https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/household-waste-recycling/recycling-glass LAST UPDATED: 24 September 2026 Glass bottles and jars from food, drinks and

LAST UPDATED: 24 September 2026 Glass bottles and jars from food, drinks and medicines can be recycled, for example pasta sauce jars, pickle jars, peanut butter jars and beer bottles. Put them in the purple-lidded glass recycling bin if you have one. If your area does not have a glass bin yet, glass bottles and jars can go in the mixed recycling

bin if you have one. If your area does not have a glass bin yet, glass bottles and jars can go in the mixed recycling bin. Before recycling glass bottles and jars, scrape out food and give them a quick rinse, and keep them loose rather than in bags. Whether lids stay on or come off depends on the council, so check your local council website.

rather than in bags. Whether lids stay on or come off depends on the council, so check your local council website. Drinking glasses, mirrors, window glass, baking dishes, ceramics, crockery and perfume bottles cannot go in any recycling bin, including the glass bin, because they melt at a different temperature to bottles and jars. Put broken

recycling bin, including the glass bin, because they melt at a different temperature to bottles and jars. Put broken drinking glasses and similar household glassware in the general rubbish bin. Glass is collected separately because small pieces of broken glass get stuck in paper, cardboard and plastic and spoil those materials. Making glass from

small pieces of broken glass get stuck in paper, cardboard and plastic and spoil those materials. Making glass from recycled glass uses around 20 to 30 percent less energy than making it from virgin sand.

foil into a ball at least the size of a tennis ball first. Empty and rinse cans and keep them loose, not in bags. Pots, pans, cutlery and other metal household items are not accepted in the mixed recycling bin; donate usable ones, and put unusable ones in the general rubbish bin. Paper and cardboard go in the mixed recycling bin. Remove food,

ones, and put unusable ones in the general rubbish bin. Paper and cardboard go in the mixed recycling bin. Remove food, flatten boxes and keep paper dry. such as a greasy pizza box, are not accepted in mixed recycling. For shredded paper and wrapping paper, check your council's rules. Hard plastics commonly accepted in mixed recycling include milk, juice and water bottles, yoghurt and ice cream tubs, fruit punnets, biscuit trays, and shampoo and soap bottles. Rules for hard plastics vary between

and ice cream tubs, fruit punnets, biscuit trays, and shampoo and soap bottles. Rules for hard plastics vary between councils because recycling facilities accept different materials. Empty and rinse containers and keep them loose, never inside plastic bags. Soft plastics are plastics you can scrunch into a ball, such as plastic bags, chip packets

never inside plastic bags. Soft plastics are plastics you can scrunch into a ball, such as plastic bags, chip packets and the outer wrappers of biscuit packets. Soft plastics generally go in the general rubbish bin. Some councils run soft plastic kerbside trials or drop-off points, and a growing number of supermarkets collect soft plastics again.

run soft plastic kerbside trials or drop-off points, and a growing number of supermarkets collect soft plastics again. Clothing and textiles must not go in recycling bins because they get caught in equipment at recycling facilities. Donate, give away or sell clothing in good condition, repair items with minor damage, turn damaged items into

Donate, give away or sell clothing in good condition, repair items with minor damage, turn damaged items into cleaning rags, or use a textile collection service or drop-off point. Recycling symbols: the Mobius loop of three arrows does not always mean an item is accepted in household recycling bins. Plastic codes 1 and 2 are commonly accepted,

does not always mean an item is accepted in household recycling bins. Plastic codes 1 and 2 are commonly accepted, code 5 is accepted by some councils, and codes 3, 4, 6 and 7 are less commonly accepted. On the Australasian Recycling Label, a solid recycling symbol means recycling bin, a transparent recycling symbol means follow the directions

Label, a solid recycling symbol means recycling bin, a transparent recycling symbol means follow the directions (often store drop-off), and a bin symbol means general rubbish bin. Container deposit scheme: eligible glass, plastic and metal drink containers can be returned for a 10-cent refund through CDS Vic.

wrapping and meat trays, cling wrap, resealable sandwich bags, containers, and takeaway packaging and utensils. straws and cutlery. If packaging and other rubbish go into the FOGO bin, the compost becomes contaminated and may be sent to landfill. To use the FOGO bin well, collect scraps in a small kitchen caddy, such as a reused ice cream tub, and empty it into the FOGO bin when full. To reduce smells and pests, keep the bin in the shade with the lid

cream tub, and empty it into the FOGO bin when full. To reduce smells and pests, keep the bin in the shade with the lid closed, freeze smelly scraps and add them the day before collection, and layer garden clippings between food scraps. Food scraps and garden clippings should only go in the general rubbish bin if you have no FOGO bin and no

food scraps. Food scraps and garden clippings should only go in the general rubbish bin if you have no FOGO bin and no composting system such as a compost bin, worm farm or bokashi system. mix with other chemicals. Never pour chemicals down the drain, where they pollute the environment and can contaminate the water supply. TITLE: Victoria's 4-bin recycling system SOURCE ORGANISATION: Sustainability Victoria (Victorian Government) SOURCE PAGE: Victoria's 4-bin recycling system LAST UPDATED: 21 August 2025 Victoria's household waste system uses four main streams: - Lime green: food and garden organics (FOGO). - Purple: glass bottles and jars. - Yellow: mixed

four main streams: - Lime green: food and garden organics (FOGO). - Purple: glass bottles and jars. - Yellow: mixed recycling. - Red: general rubbish. Separate glass collection reduces contamination in mixed recycling. Food scraps and garden clippings can be separated from landfill waste and processed into compost. Check local council guidance
and garden clippings can be separated from landfill waste and processed into compost. Check local council guidance because rollout and accepted materials can vary.

and recycling in Victoria SOURCE URL: https://www.environment.vic.gov.au/household-waste-recycling/kerbside-reform LAST UPDATED: 24 September 2026 Victoria is moving every council to a standard 4-stream household waste and recycling system by 2030. system by 2030. The four streams are food and garden organics (FOGO) with a lime green lid, glass recycling with a purple lid, mixed recycling with a yellow lid, and general rubbish with a red lid. The general rubbish bin has a red lid. Everything in the general rubbish bin goes straight to landfill without sorting. Councils pay a landfill levy on

lid. Everything in the general rubbish bin goes straight to landfill without sorting. Councils pay a landfill levy on this waste, so keeping food scraps, garden clippings and recyclables out of the red-lid bin reduces costs for ratepayers. The mixed recycling bin has a yellow lid and takes accepted plastic, metal, paper and cardboard items. So far 65 of Victoria's 79 councils have introduced a FOGO service. what is in a general rubbish bin. Once a FOGO service is available in an area, food scraps and garden clippings are no longer accepted in the general rubbish bin. and 27 of them provide a purple-lidded kerbside glass bin. Once a separate glass service is available in an area, glass is no longer accepted in the mixed recycling bin. waste provider instead of the council service. Residents there should ask their building manager, owners corporation or waste provider what applies. Victoria's target is to divert 80% of waste from landfill by 2030.
